questions.question: Find the security vulnerability in this Terraform snippet.
questions.explanation: Line 6 (`cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]`) opens SSH to the entire internet, inviting brute‑force attacks. Restrict to a specific admin IP range.

questions.question: Locate the misconfiguration that makes this S3 bucket publicly readable.
questions.explanation: Line 5 (`"Principal": "*"`) allows anyone (anonymous users) to read objects. Remove the wildcard principal or restrict to specific AWS accounts.

questions.question: Identify the dangerous permission in this IAM policy.
questions.explanation: Line 6 (`"Resource": "*"`) allows passing any role to any service – a classic privilege escalation path. Always restrict `iam:PassRole` to specific roles.

questions.question: Spot the vulnerability in this Python script that uploads a file to S3.
questions.codeSnippet:
import boto3
s3 = boto3.client('s3')
s3.put_object(Bucket='my-bucket', Key='data.csv', Body=open('data.csv', 'rb'), ACL='public-read')
questions.explanation: Line 2 uses `ACL='public-read'`, making the uploaded file world‑readable. Remove the ACL parameter to use the default (private) or enforce bucket policies.

questions.question: Find the flaw in this Network ACL (NACL) rule.
questions.explanation: Line 7 (`cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"`) combined with all ports (`from_port`/`to_port` = 0) allows any inbound traffic from anywhere. Restrict the CIDR and ports.

questions.question: Which line introduces an infrastructure misconfiguration in this AWS CLI command?
questions.explanation: Line 3 (`--cidr 0.0.0.0/0`) opens the MySQL port to the entire internet. Replace with a restricted CIDR, e.g., your VPC or a specific IP.
